toastSpeech.title: Korean Toast Speeches
toastSpeech.description: Make a toast for year-end parties, team dinners, New Year gatherings and farewells, and browse short Korean toast chants with their meanings and call-and-response lines.

make.title: Make a toast
make.description: Pick the occasion, tone and length to get a toast that flows from an opener to a few words to the chant. Toasts are written in Korean from hand-written sentences. Press 'Show other messages' for a new mix.

chants.title: {count} short toast chants
chants.description: Popular Korean acronym chants and four-character idioms, each with its meaning and call-and-response lines. The leader calls the first line and everyone answers with the second.
chants.split: Leader and group say different lines

sohwaje.meaning: Short for 소통과 화합이 제일, “communication and harmony come first.” A safe pick for team dinners and client gatherings.

mamuri.meaning: From 마음먹은 대로 무엇이든 이루자, “may we achieve whatever we set our minds to.” The word itself means “wrapping up,” so it suits year-end parties.
mamuri.lead: 마음먹은 대로! (Whatever we set our minds to!)

byeonsatto.meaning: Short for 변함없는 사랑으로 또 만나자, “let’s meet again with unchanging love.” Good for reunions with friends or family.

cheongbaji.meaning: Means 청춘은 바로 지금부터, “youth starts right now” (the word also means “blue jeans”). It lifts the mood when ages and ranks are mixed.

ojingeo.meaning: Short for 오래도록 징그럽게 어울리자, “let’s stick together for ages, almost too much” (the word means “squid”). Always gets a laugh among close friends.

dangnagwi.meaning: Short for 당신과 나의 귀한 만남을 위하여, “to the precious meeting of you and me” (the word means “donkey”). Works well with new clients or newcomers.
dangnagwi.reply: 귀한 만남을 위하여! (To our precious meeting!)

nagaja.meaning: Short for 나라와 가정과 자신의 발전을 위하여, “to the growth of our country, our families and ourselves.” Fits formal company events with many seniors.
nagaja.lead: 나라와 가정과 자신의! (Country, family and self!)

jaegeonchuk.meaning: Means 재미있고 건강하게 축복받으며 살자, “let’s live with fun, health and blessings” (the word means “rebuilding”). Good for family and old friends.

sauna.meaning: Short for 사랑과 우정을 나누자, “let’s share love and friendship.” Suits relaxed clubs and peer gatherings.

usaengsun.meaning: Short for 우리 생애 최고의 순간, “the best moment of our lives.” Great after a finished project or a good year.

wonderful.meaning: Packs 원하는 것보다 더 잘 풀리자, “may things go even better than we hope,” into the English word. Easy to use anywhere.
wonderful.reply: 더 잘 풀리자! (May it all go well!)

dangsinMeotjyeo.meaning: The first syllables of 당당하게, 신나게, 멋지게, 져 주며 살자, “live proudly, joyfully, stylishly, and be willing to give in.” It also reads as “you’re awesome,” so it lands at any gathering.

madangbal.meaning: Short for 마주 앉은 당신의 발전을 위하여, “to the success of you across the table” (the word means a well-connected person). Honors clients and partners.
madangbal.lead: 마주 앉은 당신의! (To you across the table!)

tongtongtong.meaning: Wishes for three kinds of 통: 의사소통 (communication), 운수대통 (great luck) and 만사형통 (everything going well). Good for project kickoffs and client dinners.

jujeonja.meaning: The first syllables of 주인의식 (ownership), 전문성 (expertise) and 자신감 (confidence); the word means “kettle.” Fits welcome parties and workshops.

remember.meaning: A pun on “remember this member”: let’s remember this group just as it is. Perfect for a last gathering before a team splits up or graduates.

ppappitta.meaning: Short for 빠지지 말고, 삐지지 말고, 따지지 말자, “don’t skip, don’t sulk, don’t nitpick.” A fun one for clubs that meet often.
ppappitta.lead: 빠지지 말고! 삐지지 말고! (Don’t skip! Don’t sulk!)

naiyagara.meaning: Sounds like Niagara and means 나이야, 가라, “age, go away”: forget your age and stay young. Popular at reunions and with older guests.

gugupalpal.meaning: Means “to 99, full of life” (팔팔 = lively). Suits family gatherings with elders and birthday dinners.

gahwamansaseong.meaning: An old saying: when the home is at peace, everything goes well. Good for holidays and family year-end dinners.

ilchwiwoljang.meaning: A four-character idiom for growing day by day, month by month. Good at New Year dinners and new team kickoffs.

gojingamnae.meaning: A four-character idiom: after hardship comes joy. Fits a year-end party for a team that got through a tough year.

songguyeongsin.meaning: A four-character idiom: see off the old year and welcome the new. Works from late-December parties to early-January dinners.

dongbanseongjang.meaning: Means growing together by helping each other. A good chant for wrapping up the year with clients and partners.

jihwaja.meaning: A traditional cheer that lifts the mood. The leader calls “지화자!” and everyone answers “좋다!”; elders especially love it.

wihayeo.meaning: The most basic Korean toast, meaning “to…”. Swap 우리의 내일을 in the lead for the occasion, such as 우리 팀의 내년을 (our team’s next year) or 두 분의 앞날을 (the couple’s future).

geonbae.meaning: The hanja literally means “empty the cup,” but today it simply means “cheers.” You don’t have to finish your drink, and it’s the safest choice when nothing else comes to mind.

yearEnd.meaning: A year-end chant thanking everyone for the year’s hard work. It’s in polite form, so it works with seniors present.
yearEnd.lead: 올 한 해도! (For this whole year!)
yearEnd.reply: 고생 많았습니다! (Thank you for your hard work!)

newYear.meaning: A first-toast chant for New Year dinners, wishing everyone good fortune. Natural until mid-January and around Seollal.

farewell.meaning: Cheers on someone leaving at a farewell party: “walk only on paths of flowers.” Add the person’s name before the lead to make it personal.

friendship.meaning: For reunions and longtime friends. If it’s been years, follow it with 변사또.

guide.title: How to give a good toast

whatIs.title: What is a Korean toast speech?
whatIs.description: A Korean toast speech (건배사) briefly says why everyone is gathered before glasses go up, then brings the room together with a chant everyone shouts. A short, easy-to-follow chant is remembered longer than a long, polished speech. On this page you can make a toast for your occasion and pick from short chants commonly used at Korean dinners and gatherings.

howToUse.title: Toast order: opener → a few words → chant
items: Opener: get attention with something like “Could everyone fill their glasses?” and wait until all glasses are raised.
A few words: sum up the year or today’s reason for gathering in one or two sentences. Mentioning a name or something you went through together makes it sincere.
Teach the chant: tell people the response first, such as “When I say 소통과 화합이!, please answer 제일!”.
Chant: call the lead loudly, let everyone answer with the response, then clink glasses.
Keep the whole thing under 30 seconds. About 150 Korean characters read aloud, three sentences and one chant, is plenty.

tips.title: Getting the call and response right
items: Always announce the response once before you start. Nobody can follow a chant they’ve never heard.
Shorter responses work better. Two- or three-syllable answers like 제일! or 멋져! come back loud and together.
Call the lead louder and slower than usual, rising at the end, so everyone knows when to answer.
With a big group, count “one, two, three” and raise your glass as a signal so the response doesn’t scatter.
Asked out of the blue? A quick 위하여 or 건배 is perfectly fine.

realWorld.title: Tips by occasion
items: Year-end party: thank everyone for the year first, then end with a wish for next year. 마무리, 고진감래 and 송구영신 fit well.
New Year dinner: keep last year short and focus on resolutions. 일취월장, 통통통 and 새해 복 많이 are common.
Farewell party: name one thing you did with the person leaving and cheer on their future. Support comes before regret. 꽃길만 걷자 and 이 멤버 리멤버 work well.
With clients: thank the other company first, then talk about the year ahead together. 마당발, 동반성장 and 당나귀 are safe picks.
Family gatherings: wishes for health and harmony get the warmest response. Try 구구팔팔, 가화만사성 or 지화자.

comparison.title: What to avoid in front of clients and bosses
items: Leave out anything that pushes drinking, such as “bottoms up.” Raising a glass is enough.
Jokes about someone’s looks, age, marriage or mistakes can hurt even when meant in fun.
Don’t bring up sales pressure, complaints about the company, politics or religion.
Avoid acronym chants that can be read sexually, no matter how popular they are.
At a client dinner, a long boast about your own company is rude. Thank the other side first.
With bosses present, give the opener and your few words in polite speech, and pick a chant whose meaning is obvious, like 위하여, over a casual joke chant.

items.q: How long should a toast be?
items.a: Under 30 seconds. One sentence of greeting, one or two about why you’re gathered, and one chant is plenty. Any longer and people holding their glasses get tired and the chant loses energy.

items.q: What are the lead and the response?
items.a: The lead (선창) is what the person proposing the toast calls first, and the response (후창) is what everyone else shouts back together. For 소화제, the lead is 소통과 화합이! and the response is 제일!. Announcing the response once before you start keeps everyone in sync.

items.q: What about people who don’t drink?
items.a: They can raise a glass of water or a soft drink. A toast is about raising glasses together, not about drinking. If the person proposing adds “Feel free to join with any drink,” everyone can take part comfortably.

items.q: What should I say if I’m suddenly asked to give a toast?
items.a: Two sentences, “Thank you all for your hard work this year. I hope we gather again next year with smiles,” plus 위하여! is enough. Choose “Short” in the toast maker on this page for a line you can read right away.

Chants that honor the other side or wish shared success are safe: 마당발 (to the success of you across the table), 동반성장 (growing together) and 당나귀 (to our precious meeting). A chant whose meaning comes across right away beats a playful one.

items.q: How do year-end and New Year toasts differ?
items.a: A year-end toast thanks everyone for the past year first and ends with a wish for the next, while a New Year toast centers on resolutions and goals. Between late December and early January, a chant like 송구영신 fits both.
